description: Every year the Earth records hundreds of thousands of earthquakes. Most go unnoticed. A few change whole cities.

hero.hook: An earthquake is not a whim of the ground. It is energy that has waited far too long.

blocks.text: Every year the Earth records about **500,000 earthquakes** that instruments can detect. Only a small share cause serious damage. A quake is not random: it is the sudden end of a long build-up of energy inside the rock.
To understand it, picture the surface of the planet as a jigsaw of moving plates. Where those plates rub against each other, the strain rises, until something snaps.

The Earth's surface is cut into about a dozen large **tectonic plates**. They slide on a softer layer of the mantle, the [[asthenosphere]]. How fast? Roughly **1 to 10 cm a year**, about the speed a fingernail grows.

blocks.caption: Earthquakes release in one go the energy stored along a fault

blocks.text: At the boundaries, three situations dominate. The plates pull apart, as at the ocean ridges. They collide, and [[Subduction]] is what happens when one dives beneath the other. Or they slide side by side, as along the [[San Andreas Fault]] in California, about **1,300 km** long.
Along the San Andreas, Los Angeles is moving toward San Francisco by about **6 cm** a year. In **15 million years** the two cities would be neighbors.
It is mainly at these boundaries that earthquakes are born. Friction between rocks blocks the movement of the plates. The energy builds up in silence.
An earthquake happens along a **fault**: a fracture between two blocks of rock. In theory the plates should slide without ever stopping. In practice, friction often locks that sliding.
Meanwhile the plates keep pushing. The rock deforms a little, like a bow being drawn. This is called elastic strain. It can last for decades, sometimes for centuries.

When the limit of resistance is passed, the blocks slip all at once. The energy leaves as **seismic waves**. The point where the rock breaks, deep down, is the **focus**. At the surface, the point directly above it is the **epicenter**, where the effects are often strongest.

To measure the energy of an earthquake, seismologists mostly use the moment [[magnitude scale]]. It is logarithmic: each degree multiplies the energy by about **32**. So a magnitude **8** earthquake releases about **1,000 times** more energy than a magnitude **6** one.
There are also earthquakes of magnitude **0** or below. These are tiny events, visible only to very sensitive instruments.

The strongest ever measured with modern instruments struck **Valdivia**, in Chile, in **1960**: magnitude **9.5**. If the focus lies under the ocean and lifts the seafloor, the displaced column of water can create a **tsunami**. In **2004**, a magnitude **9.1** earthquake near Sumatra set off a tsunami that hit 14 countries and killed about **227,000** people.

sections.title: Measuring the power, fearing the tsunami

blocks.text: After the break, several kinds of waves set off. The **P waves** (primary) arrive first: they squeeze the rock like an accordion. Then come the **S waves** (secondary), slower and often more destructive. Surface waves follow and make the ground roll in a very visible way.

We still cannot predict the exact day of a big earthquake. We can, however, map the areas at risk. [[Earthquake engineering]] designs buildings that can take the shaking: sliding foundations, giant dampers, structures that soak up the energy. In Japan, early warning systems detect the P waves and can shut off the gas or slow the trains before the most dangerous waves arrive.
An earthquake is born when rocks locked along a fault release decades of strain in a single moment. The energy travels as waves, and each degree of magnitude multiplies that energy by about **32**.
